steps.content: The idea is short-term reversal: yesterday's return, negated. The simplest form is minus one times yesterday's return, using close-to-close price change so the value is unit-free and comparable across coins.

Rank IC is +0.0175 but incremental IC is exactly 0.0000 — that is the short-term reversal style that is already subtracted out. So the raw bounce measure carries no new information; I keep the direction and measure yesterday's move in a form that still overlaps the known styles but is not identical.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

A 3-day mean of the same return measure overlaps the 1-day reversal style, so it also gives 0.0000. Two attempts in a row now fail to improve on the first result, so I stop here and hand in the simplest version.

What I found: the bounce idea does hold on this history — yesterday's return is a real predictor of next-day returns, with rank IC about +0.018 and a raw rank IC of +0.0175. But the incremental part is exactly 0.0000, meaning it is entirely absorbed by the short-term reversal style that is already removed. The effect is real but short-lived, and the effect fades to nothing once the reversal style is subtracted. The direction is kept as the idea states: coins that fell a lot yesterday score high.

The idea is about dollar volume relative to the coin's own history: coins with low dollar volume should do better, so the factor should be the negative of a short average of USDT-denominated volume. I'll start with the simplest form — a 5-day mean of `quote_volume`, negated.

The simple level form works: incremental IC +0.0071 with t = 5.6, positive in every period though weaker in 2024. The idea is really about low volume being the *exception*, so I'll try a 60-day baseline to see whether the effect survives as a persistent low-volume state rather than a recent dip.

The relative form is worse (0.0096, t = 3.3) and nearly flat in 2024, so the level of dollar volume itself carries the signal rather than its deviation from a 60-day norm. That's two tests in a row that failed to improve, so I'll stop here.

What I found: negated 5-day dollar volume has rank IC +0.044 and incremental IC +0.0071 (t = 5.6), positive in all three periods but weak in 2024; the effect is a short-horizon effect, not a persistent one, since the 60-day baseline version was weaker and flat in 2024. Direction stays as the idea states — low dollar volume means a high factor value.

The idea is a one-day reversal: yesterday's return, flipped, predicts next-day return. Since it's a one-day quantity, the factor should be a short window of the negative one-day return. I'll start with the simplest form and see how much survives after the reversal style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw one-day reversal gives +0.0175 rank IC but exactly 0 incremental IC — it is fully absorbed by the short-term reversal style. So the effect lives in the known reversal term, not in new information. I need a form that captures "fell a lot" without being a literal one-day return. The natural next thing is the largest single-day drop over the last few days, which is not the same quantity as the one-day return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0140
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0081 (t = -3.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0122, 2023 -0.0100, 2024 -0.0041

The 5-day minimum of one-day drops has a real but negative incremental IC (−0.0081, negative in all three periods), so extreme single-day drops are a bearish signal here, opposite to the idea. The literal reading is the best-measured one, so I keep it and stop searching.

What I found: yesterday's return is a strong predictor (+0.0175 rank IC), but its entire effect is already explained by the short-term reversal style, so incremental IC is 0.0000. The idea holds as stated — a coin that fell a lot yesterday does bounce — but the bounce is entirely the known reversal effect, and it fades to nothing new after 1-day reversal is removed. The alternative reading (largest drop over the last five days) is actually a bearish signal on this history, so I did not flip it.

The idea is a short-horizon reversal: yesterday's return, negated. Since the factor must be unit-free and comparable across coins, I take the ratio of close to close a day ago, which is a unitless return. I'll start with the simplest form — minus one times yesterday's return, over a one-day window.

What I found: the one-day version of this idea is worth nothing after the known styles are removed, because the reversal effect is exactly a one-day return. Measured over two days, the bounce is still real and survives the style removal, with incremental IC +0.0102 (t = 4.5) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect fades as the window lengthens, so it is a short-horizon reversal, not a persistent bounce.

The idea is a short-horizon reversal: yesterday's return is the thing that predicts next-day returns, and a coin that fell a lot yesterday should do better. I'll start with the simplest version — yesterday's return, negated — using returns rather than prices so it's comparable across coins.

The 3-day window lifts the incremental IC to +0.0075 with t = 3.4 and the same sign in all three periods. Since the idea is about yesterday's fall, I'll keep the window small and try a 2-day window next.

A 2-day window gives +0.0102 (t = 4.5), an improvement of about 0.0027 over the 3-day version, but the gain is smaller than the previous one and I've used my 5 tests. I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same history.

What I found: the effect is real and points the way the idea says (bounces after a coin falls yesterday), with a rank IC of +0.032 and an incremental IC of +0.0102 after the known reversal style is removed. The signal lives in the last few days, not in yesterday alone — a 2-day window beats 3 days, and the sign is consistent in all three periods. The raw IC is much larger than the incremental one, meaning most of yesterday's reversal is already explained by the known reversal style; what remains is a genuine, if modest, short-horizon bounce.

Idea: low dollar-denominated volume is bullish, so the factor should be the negative of average USDT volume over a window. I'll start with the simplest form: a 20-day mean of `quote_volume`, negated.

The 20-day mean gives +0.0371 raw rank IC but only +0.0011 incremental (t = 1.9), and 2024 flips to slightly negative — a 20-day mean of volume is mostly a liquidity proxy. Let me try a shorter, more responsive window to see whether the effect lives in recent activity.

Shorter window helps a lot: +0.0071 incremental (t = 5.6) and positive in all three periods, though 2024 is weaker. The effect looks like recent volume matters more than the 60-day average, so I'll push the window shorter to 3 days and see whether responsiveness keeps paying.

The 3-day window is essentially tied with the 5-day one (+0.0074, t = 5.7) but more responsive, so I'll stop here rather than spend a fifth test.

What I found: the idea holds on this history — coins trading small dollar amounts go on to do better, with rank IC around +0.044 and an incremental IC of +0.0071 after the known styles are removed, t = 5.6. The effect is strongest in 2022H2 and 2023 and fades in 2024, so it is a real but decaying edge rather than a stable one. The window matters a lot: a 60-day average of dollar volume is a liquidity proxy with essentially nothing left after the styles are removed (+0.0011), while the last few days of volume capture a fresh-activity effect. The factor is negated so that small dollar volume scores high.

The idea is about dollar volume: coins with little USDT turnover should do better. I'll measure it as the average log dollar volume over a short window, since a log average keeps the measure unit-free and comparable across coins, and the negative sign makes low volume bullish.

Now I'll check whether a median instead of a mean over the same 5 days captures the "very little" part of the idea robustly, since a single huge volume day can dominate a mean.

The median version drops to +0.0043, so the mean is what carries the signal — the extreme-volume days are not the problem. That is my second failed variant in a row, so I'll stop here and keep the 5-day mean.

What I found: the idea holds on this history, but only in the short term — a 5-day average of log dollar volume has incremental IC +0.0071 (t = 5.6), with the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though it weakens in 2024. Stretching the window to 20 days destroys it (+0.0011, t = 1.9, sign flips in 2024), so the effect decays quickly; using a median instead of a mean also hurts. The direction is as the idea states: low dollar volume scores high.

What I found: the idea holds in raw form (rank IC +0.037), but only a small part survives after the known styles are removed (0.0011–0.0015), and it is weakest in 2024. The effect is a slow one — a coin that has been trading a thin dollar volume over the past month keeps outperforming, which fits the idea's wording; a single volume spike or a short window is not what carries it. I'm submitting the 20-day version, pointing the sign down as the idea says.

Only about +0.0015 of that survives the removal of the known styles, so the effect is real but small and largely absorbed by the liquidity style; the signal is persistent rather than a recent one, since a short window is worse and a long window is the best version. Measuring the level against each coin's own 20-day norm (relative change) destroyed it, which says the effect is the level itself, not a coin's recent move. The factor points the way the idea says, with the negative sign on the outside.
